abstract: Gans and Goldfarb study automation when tasks are quality complements rather than separable, using an O-ring production function where a worker's output is the product of task qualities. They show that partial automation triggers a 'focus' mechanism: when machines replace some tasks, workers concentrate their time on the remaining ones, raising quality multiplicatively. This generates three key results that challenge standard task-based automation frameworks.
keyFindings: Task-by-task substitution logic is incomplete because automating one task changes the return to automating others
Automation decisions are discrete and can require bundled adoption even when automation quality improves smoothly
Labour income can rise under partial automation because automation scales the value of remaining bottleneck tasks
Widely-used exposure indices that use linear aggregation will overstate displacement when tasks are complements
The relevant object is not average task exposure but the structure of bottlenecks and how automation reshapes worker time around them
methodology: Formal theoretical model using an O-ring (multiplicative) production function where job output equals the product of task qualities. Worker allocates fixed time endowment across n tasks; machines replace tasks at given quality theta at cost r per task. Derives conditions for when partial automation raises vs. lowers worker marginal product and labor income. No empirical data; pure analytical results from the model.
qualifiers: This is a theoretical model paper — all results are qualitative predictions from the formal framework, not empirical findings. The model assumes symmetric task structure and constant labor productivity across tasks (simplifying assumptions). The O-ring production function is one specific functional form; results may differ under alternative complementarity structures.
